source.title: A Generalist Agent
source.authors: S. Reed; Konrad Zolna; Emilio Parisotto; Sergio Gomez Colmenarejo; Alexander Novikov; Gabriel Barth-Maron; Mai Giménez; Yury Sulsky; Jackie Kay; J. Springenberg; Tom Eccles; Jake Bruce; Ali Razavi; Ashley D. Edwards; N. Heess; Yutian Chen; R. Hadsell; O. Vinyals; Mahyar Bordbar; N. de Freitas

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper varies model size and reports aggregate control performance, a different measure from held-out language-model cross-entropy loss. This bears on V6, but it does not test the claimed loss laws or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The scaling analysis in Figure 8 reports aggregate in-distribution control performance versus tokens processed for three model sizes. The paper explicitly says it does not report validation loss over held-out data because it did not correlate well with held-out task episode returns. Other performance tables and ablations do not test the claim versions recorded here.
record.test_reason: Gato is a multi-embodiment control agent (about 85% control data by sample weight), not a language model. Its only scaling analysis (Sec. 5.1, Fig. 8) plots aggregate in-distribution episode return against tokens for three sizes (79M, 364M, 1.18B). It fits no power law, reports no held-out pretraining loss, makes no extrapolation, and does not study allocation or shape. The return is on the training tasks themselves, not on downstream tasks. So it measures a related construct: control-task return of an agent policy versus size. This goes under fits_no_version, not as a test of V5 or V6. Scaling-law language elsewhere (intro, conclusion) is citation and projection.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' main conclusion is that transformer sequence models are effective multi-task, multi-embodiment policies and promising for few-shot adaptation. The statement that performance 'will increase with scale' is a projection from cited scaling-law trends. Their own evidence is the three-size return curve, not a fitted law.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a three-size model sweep and aggregate in-distribution control returns rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy, fitted loss power laws, or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Model size and training-token count are varied; the paper reports higher aggregate performance at equivalent token counts for larger models.

fits_no_version.finding: For a fixed token count, aggregate in-distribution control return rises with model size across 79M, 364M and 1.18B. The authors call this a consistent improvement (Fig. 8). No fit or numbers are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Control/agent return of multi-task transformer policies improves monotonically with parameter count at fixed tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: In simulated RGB-stacking fine-tuning, larger models adapt better with fewer episodes (Fig. 10 right). The 79M model is clearly worse, and the 364M model overfits on one episode.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Few-shot fine-tuning performance of generalist agents improves with model size, with non-monotonic exceptions at very low data.

fits_no_version.finding: The model card says held-out validation loss 'did not correlate well with episode return' on held-out tasks. No numbers are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In multi-task agent training, validation loss is a poor predictor of held-out task return.

record.problems: The scaling result is based on three model sizes and aggregate task performance; the numerical curve values are only shown in Figure 8. The authors do not report held-out validation loss, and the model card says reported values do not account for model uncertainty because they evaluate a single model.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the tested version were left out; other reported task evaluations and ablations do not measure scale-related predictability as defined by the versions.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute is reported. The authors chose not to report validation loss.
No fitted law and no extrapolation to larger runs.
The three sizes differ in shape as well as size. There is no fixed-size shape comparison.
There is no power-law form for agent or multimodal loss or performance. Only three monotone points of return are shown.
Downstream LM task performance versus scale or loss, and any quantitative prediction.
Fitting choices and bending of curves.

missing.what: Model-size ablation of few-shot fine-tuning on simulated Skill Generalization (1.18B vs 364M vs 79M). It shows scale helps, except that 364M overfits at one episode.
missing.locator: Section 5.3 'Fine-tuning and Model Size', Figure 10 right

missing.what: Statement that validation loss did not correlate well with held-out episode return.
missing.versions: none (bears loosely on V6 loss-based predictability, but for an agent, not an LM)

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' label is dropped. The system is an agent policy and the measure is in-distribution return, with only three sizes and no fit, so it does not bear on downstream predictability as the versions define it. The model sizes also vary depth, width, heads and key size together (Table 5), and learning rates differ across sizes (Table 6). No uncertainty is reported, and each point is a single model.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, and compute; power-law form and range.
Whether loss laws fitted on smaller runs predict much larger runs.
The compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss in other modalities or training regimes; multimodal task performance is not a test of the claimed loss form.
The study reports an aggregate control-performance trend, not fitted predictions, per-task downstream scaling laws, or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
Whether exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on setup or fitting choices, or curves bend away from a power law.
